newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - Daimler denies report on job cuts.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Daimler denies report on job cuts.

text.p: Daimler-Benz AG on Monday denied comments at the weekend from a top union leader that the German industrial group planned to cut about 23,000 jobs in the coming years.
Daimler said in a statement that it expected a stable employment situation in 1997 and saw no reason for major changes in its workforce in the coming years.
The union official who made the comments, IG Metall deputy chairman, Walter Riester, had "misspoken" about the job cuts at Daimler, an IG Metall spokesman said on Monday.
"Comments about plans to cut 23,000 jobs at Daimler-Benz are false," Daimler management board member Heiner Tropitzsch, who is responsible for personnel issues, said in a statement.
"There are no such plans," he said, adding that the statements at the weekend had been due to a misunderstanding.
"For the foreseeable coming years, we see no reason for this situation to change," he said.
Riester said in a newspaper interview published on Sunday that the 23,000 jobs would be cut by the turn of the century.

Riester also told the Berliner Zeitung that Daimler, maker of Mercedes vehicles and also a key player in the aerospace industry, planned to boost sales by 26 percent by 1999 but that its payroll would have to be cut by eight percent.
Tropitzsch said he stood by his statements at Daimler's annual news conference in early April at which he said the worst of Daimler's job cuts were over.
At the end of 1996 Daimler had about 290,000 employees around the world, about 21,000 less than at the end of 1995, and far below the 380,000 employees at Daimler in 1991.
The cuts were mostly due to restructuring measures, which included last year disposing of troubled electronics group AEG and Dutch aircraft maker Fokker NV.
Daimler plans to cut about 3,200 jobs in 1997 through the sale of former units of AEG.
Riester's comments prompted one top German politician, Research Minister Juergen Ruettgers, on Monday to question whether Bonn must step forward and stop job cuts.
If the reported comments by Riester were correct, Ruettgers told German radio network Suedwestfunk: "Then the government must say enough is enough."
